title: Second law of thermodynamics
description: Physical law for entropy and heat
wiki_lead:
The second law of thermodynamics is a physical law based on universal empirical observation concerning heat and energy interconversions. A simple statement of the law is that heat always flows spontaneously from hotter to colder regions of matter (or 'downhill' in terms of the temperature gradient). Another statement is: "Not all heat can be converted into work in a cyclic process." These are informal definitions, however; more formal definitions appear below.
The second law of thermodynamics establishes the concept of entropy as a physical property of a thermodynamic system. It predicts whether processes are forbidden despite obeying the requirement of conservation of energy as expressed in the first law of thermodynamics and provides necessary criteria for spontaneous processes. For example, the first law allows the process of a cup falling off a table and breaking on the floor, as well as allowing the reverse process of the cup fragments coming back together and 'jumping' back onto the table, while the second law allows the former and denies the latter. The second law may be formulated by the observation that the entropy of isolated systems left to spontaneous evolution cannot decrease, as they always tend toward a state of thermodynamic equilibrium where the entropy is highest at the given internal energy. An increase in the combined entropy of system and surroundings accounts for the irreversibility of natural processes, often referred to in the concept of the arrow of time.
Historically, the second law was an empirical finding that was accepted as an axiom of thermodynamic theory. Statistical mechanics provides a microscopic explanation of the law in terms of probability distributions of the states of large assemblies of atoms or molecules. The second law has been expressed in many ways. Its first formulation, which preceded the proper definition of entropy and was based on caloric theory, is Carnot's theorem, formulated by the French scientist Sadi Carnot, who in 1824 showed that the efficiency of conversion of heat to work in a heat engine has an upper limit. The first rigorous definition of the second law based on the concept of entropy came from German scientist Rudolf Clausius in the 1850s and included his statement that heat can never pass from a colder to a warmer body without some other change, connected therewith, occurring at the same time.
The second law of thermodynamics allows the definition of the concept of thermodynamic temperature, but this has been formally delegated to the zeroth law of thermodynamics.

Introduction

grok_lead: The second law of thermodynamics is a fundamental physical law that asserts the entropy of an isolated system cannot decrease over time; it either increases for irreversible processes or remains constant for reversible ones, thereby defining the directionality of spontaneous natural processes. This law emerged in the mid-19th century as scientists sought to explain the limitations of heat engines beyond the conservation of energy encapsulated in the first law. In 1854, German physicist Rudolf Clausius formulated one key statement: it is impossible for heat to flow spontaneously from a colder body to a hotter body without external work. In 1851, British physicist William Thomson (later Lord Kelvin) provided an equivalent formulation: no process is possible whose sole result is the absorption of heat from a reservoir and its complete conversion into work. These statements are mathematically equivalent, as violating one allows construction of a device that violates the other, such as a perpetual motion machine of the second kind. Clausius later introduced the concept of entropy in 1865 as a quantitative measure of disorder or unavailable energy, defined for a reversible process as $ dS = \frac{dQ_{\text{rev}}}{T} $, where $ dQ_{\text{rev}} $ is the reversible heat transfer and $ T $ is the absolute temperature. For any real process, the second law implies $ \Delta S_{\text{universe}} \geq 0 $, with equality only in reversible cases, underscoring the irreversibility inherent in natural phenomena like diffusion, friction, and heat conduction. Among its profound implications, the second law establishes the maximum efficiency of heat engines, as given by the Carnot efficiency $ \eta = 1 - \frac{T_c}{T_h} $, where $ T_c $ and $ T_h $ are the cold and hot reservoir temperatures, respectively, preventing any engine from achieving 100% efficiency. It also provides an arrow of time, distinguishing past from future by the increase in entropy, and predicts the eventual "heat death" of the universe as a state of maximum entropy. Despite its name, the law's validity is not limited to thermodynamics: in broader applications, the law governs chemical reactions via Gibbs free energy, biological processes, and even information theory, influencing fields from engineering to cosmology.
